chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Soon after his admission to the Masonic Brotherhood, Pierre went to the Kiev province, where he had the greatest number of serfs, carrying with him detailed instructions he had written for his own guidance on what to do with his estates.

When he reached Kiev, he summoned all his stewards to the head office and laid out his intentions and wishes. He told them that steps would be taken immediately to free his serfs — and until then, they were not to be overworked, nursing mothers were not to be sent to labor, assistance was to be given to the serfs, punishments were to be educational rather than physical, and hospitals, asylums, and schools were to be established on all the estates. Some of the stewards — among them semi-literate foremen — listened with alarm, supposing these words meant the young count was unhappy with their management and their embezzlement. Some, after their initial fright, were amused by Pierre's lisp and the unfamiliar words. Others simply enjoyed hearing the master talk. But the cleverest among them, including the chief steward, understood from this speech exactly how to manage the master for their own benefit.

The chief steward expressed great sympathy with Pierre's plans, but pointed out that besides these changes it would be necessary to review the overall state of affairs, which was far from satisfactory.

Despite Count Bezukhov's enormous wealth — since he had come into an income reportedly amounting to five hundred thousand rubles a year — Pierre felt himself far poorer than when his father had given him an allowance of ten thousand. He had a rough sense of the following budget:

About 80,000 went in payments on all the estates to the Land Bank; about 30,000 for the upkeep of the Moscow estate, the town house, and allowances to the three princesses; about 15,000 in pensions and the same for asylums; 150,000 in alimony to the countess; about 70,000 for interest on debts. Construction of a new church, previously begun, had cost about 10,000 in each of the last two years, and he didn't know how the rest — about 100,000 rubles — was spent. Almost every year he had to borrow. Besides this, the chief steward wrote annually about fires and bad harvests, or about the need to rebuild factories and workshops. So the first task Pierre faced was one for which he had very little talent or inclination — practical business.

He discussed estate affairs every day with his chief steward, but felt that none of it moved anything forward. He sensed that these consultations were disconnected from real life and didn't make things happen. On one hand, the chief steward painted the worst possible picture, emphasizing the need to pay off debts and undertake new projects with serf labor — to which Pierre wouldn't agree. On the other hand, Pierre demanded that steps be taken to liberate the serfs, which the steward deflected by pointing out that the Land Bank loans must be paid off first, making immediate emancipation impossible.

The steward didn't say outright that it couldn't be done, but suggested selling the forests in Kostroma province, the land along the lower river, and the Crimean estate — all of which involved, according to him, such complicated procedures — injunctions, petitions, permits, and so on — that Pierre became thoroughly bewildered and could only reply:
"Yes, yes, do that."

Pierre lacked the practical persistence needed to manage the business himself, so he disliked it and only pretended to the steward that he was paying attention. The steward, for his part, pretended to the count that these consultations were extremely valuable for the proprietor and troublesome for himself.

In Kiev, Pierre encountered some people he knew, and strangers rushed to make the acquaintance of the rich newcomer, the largest landowner in the province. Temptations targeting Pierre's greatest weakness — the one he had confessed at his Lodge initiation — were so powerful that he couldn't resist them. Once again whole days, weeks, and months passed in a blur of evening parties, dinners, lunches, and balls, leaving him no time for reflection — just like in Petersburg. Instead of the new life he had planned, he was living the same old life, only in different surroundings.

Of the three Masonic precepts, Pierre realized he was failing the one that required every Mason to set an example of moral living, and of the seven virtues he lacked two: morality and the love of death. He consoled himself with the thought that he was fulfilling another precept — reforming humanity — and possessed other virtues: love of his neighbor and especially generosity.

In the spring of 1807 he decided to return to Petersburg. On the way, he planned to visit all his estates and see for himself how his orders had been carried out, and what condition the serfs were in — the serfs God had entrusted to his care and whom he intended to help.

The chief steward, who considered the young count's schemes nearly insane — unprofitable for himself, for the count, and for the serfs — had made some concessions. While continuing to represent the liberation of the serfs as impractical, he arranged for large buildings — schools, hospitals, and asylums — to be erected on all the estates before the master arrived. Everywhere preparations were made, not for ceremonious welcomes (which he knew Pierre wouldn't like), but for touchingly religious ones, with offerings of icons and the bread and salt of hospitality — just the kind that, in his understanding of the master, would impress and deceive him.

The southern spring, the comfortable, rapid travel in a Viennese carriage, and the solitude of the road all had a cheering effect on Pierre. His estates — which he had never visited before — were each more picturesque than the last; the serfs everywhere seemed thriving and touchingly grateful for the benefits conferred on them. Everywhere there were receptions, which, though they embarrassed Pierre, stirred a joyful feeling deep in his heart. In one place the peasants presented him with bread, salt, and an icon of Saints Peter and Paul, and asked permission — as a mark of gratitude — to build a new chapel at their own expense in honor of his patron saints. In another, the women with babies came to thank him for releasing them from hard labor. On a third estate, the priest came to meet him bearing a cross, surrounded by children whom — thanks to the count's generosity — he was teaching reading, writing, and religion. On all his estates Pierre saw brick buildings either completed or under construction, all built to the same plan, for hospitals, schools, and almshouses — which were due to open soon. Everywhere he saw the stewards' accounts showing that the serfs' compulsory labor had been reduced, and heard the grateful speeches of deputations of serfs in their best blue coats.

What Pierre did not know was this: the place where they presented him with bread and salt and wanted to build a chapel in honor of Peter and Paul was a market village where a fair was held on Saint Peter's Day, and that the richest peasants (who made up the deputation) had started building the chapel long before; nine-tenths of the peasants in that village were in extreme poverty. He did not know that since the nursing mothers were no longer sent to work on his land, they now did even harder work on their own. He did not know that the priest who met him with the cross was squeezing the peasants for fees, and that the pupils' parents wept at having to give up their children, paying heavily to get them back. He did not know that the brick buildings, built to a uniform plan, were being constructed by serf labor — increasing their workload, even though it had been reduced on paper. He did not know that where the steward's accounts showed a one-third reduction in the serfs' payments, their obligatory estate labor had been increased by half. And so Pierre was delighted with his visit to his estates and wrote enthusiastic letters to his "brother-instructor," as he called the Grand Master.
"How easy it is, how little effort it takes, to do so much good," thought Pierre, "and how little attention we pay to it!"
He was pleased by the gratitude he received but felt awkward about it. The gratitude reminded him of how much more he could do for these simple, kind people.

The chief steward — a very stupid but cunning man who saw right through the naive and intelligent count and played him like a toy — observing the effect of these staged receptions, pressed him even harder with arguments about the impossibility and especially the pointlessness of freeing the serfs, who were perfectly happy as they were.

Pierre secretly agreed with the steward that it would be hard to imagine happier people, and God only knew what would happen to them when they were free — but he insisted, though reluctantly, on what he believed was right. The steward promised to do everything in his power to carry out the count's wishes, knowing perfectly well that not only would the count never check whether the forests had actually been sold or the Land Bank loans paid off, but would probably never even ask — and would never find out that the newly built buildings stood empty and that the serfs continued to hand over, in money and labor, everything that could be squeezed from them.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: Returning from his tour of southern Russia in the happiest frame of mind, Pierre carried out an intention he had long had — visiting his friend Bolkonski, whom he hadn't seen in two years.

Bogucharovo lay in a flat, uninteresting stretch of country among fields and forests of fir and birch, partly cut down. The house stood behind a newly dug pond, filled to the brim, its banks still bare. It was at the end of a village that stretched along the highway, in the middle of a young copse dotted with a few fir trees.

The homestead consisted of a threshing floor, outbuildings, stables, a bathhouse, a lodge, and a large brick house with a semicircular facade, still under construction. Around it was a newly laid-out garden. The fences and gates were new and solid; two fire pumps and a water cart, painted green, stood in a shed; the paths were straight, the bridges strong and had handrails. Everything bore the stamp of tidiness and good management. Some household serfs Pierre met, in reply to his question about where the prince lived, pointed to a small, recently built lodge near the pond. Anton, the man who had looked after Prince Andrew since childhood, helped Pierre out of his carriage, said the prince was home, and showed him into a clean little anteroom.
Pierre was struck by the modesty of the small but clean house after the grand surroundings in which he had last seen his friend in Petersburg.
He quickly entered the little reception room with its still-unplastered wooden walls, fragrant with pine, and would have gone farther, but Anton ran ahead on tiptoe and knocked at a door.
"Well, what is it?" came a sharp, unpleasant voice.
"A visitor," Anton answered.
"Ask him to wait," and the sound of a chair being pushed back was heard.

Pierre walked quickly to the door and came face to face with Prince Andrew, who emerged frowning and looking older. Pierre embraced him and, lifting his spectacles, kissed his friend on the cheek and studied him closely.
"Well, I didn't expect you — but I'm very glad," said Prince Andrew.

Pierre said nothing; he stared at his friend in surprise. He was struck by the change in him. His words were kind and there was a smile on his lips, but his eyes were dull and lifeless, and despite an obvious wish to appear otherwise, he couldn't give them a joyful, glad sparkle. Prince Andrew had grown thinner, paler, and more manly, but what startled and estranged Pierre — until he got used to it — were his apathy and a deep crease on his brow, the mark of prolonged concentration on a single thought.

As usually happens when people meet after a long separation, their conversation was slow to settle on anything. They asked questions and gave brief answers about topics they knew should be discussed at length. Eventually the talk gradually found its footing, touching on their past, their plans, Pierre's travels and activities, the war, and so on. The preoccupation and gloom Pierre had noticed in his friend's expression were now even more evident in the smile with which he listened — especially when Pierre spoke with happy excitement about the past or the future. It was as if Prince Andrew wanted to sympathize with what Pierre was saying but couldn't. Pierre began to feel it was in poor taste to talk about his enthusiasms, dreams, and hopes for happiness in Prince Andrew's presence. He was embarrassed to share his new Masonic views, which his recent travels had especially strengthened. He held himself back, afraid of seeming naive; and yet he felt an irresistible desire to show his friend as soon as possible that he was now a completely different and better Pierre than the one Prince Andrew had known in Petersburg.
"I can't tell you how much I've lived through since then. I hardly recognize myself."
"Yes, we've changed a great deal — very much — since then," said Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you? What are your plans?"
"Plans!" Prince Andrew repeated ironically. "My plans?" he said, as though astonished by the word. "Well, you see, I'm building. I plan to settle here for good next year..."
Pierre looked silently and searchingly into Prince Andrew's face, which had aged considerably.
"No, I meant to ask..." Pierre began, but Prince Andrew interrupted.
"But why talk about me? Tell me about yourself — about your travels and everything you've been doing on your estates."

Pierre began describing what he had done on his estates, trying as much as possible to downplay his own role in the improvements. Prince Andrew several times prompted Pierre's account, as though it were all an old, familiar story, and he listened not only without interest but as if embarrassed by what Pierre was telling him.
Pierre began to feel uncomfortable and even depressed in his friend's company, and at last fell silent.

"I'll tell you what, my dear fellow," said Prince Andrew — who also clearly felt awkward and constrained with his visitor — "I'm only camping out here and just came to look things over. I'm going back to my sister today. I'll introduce you to her. Though of course you know her already," he added, obviously trying to entertain a guest with whom he now had nothing in common. "We'll go after dinner. And would you like to look around the place now?"

They went out and walked about until dinnertime, talking about political news and mutual acquaintances like people who aren't close. Prince Andrew spoke with some energy and interest only about the new house and its construction; but even then, while standing on the scaffolding in the middle of explaining the future layout, he suddenly broke off:
"Anyway, this isn't interesting at all. Let's have dinner, and then we'll set off."
At dinner the conversation turned to Pierre's marriage.
"I was very surprised when I heard about it," said Prince Andrew.
Pierre blushed, as he always did when the subject came up, and said hurriedly: "I'll tell you someday how it all happened. But you know it's over — and forever."
"Forever?" said Prince Andrew. "Nothing is forever."
"But you know how it ended, don't you? You heard about the duel?"
"Yes, so you had to go through that too!"
"One thing I thank God for is that I didn't kill that man," said Pierre.
"Why?" asked Prince Andrew. "Killing a vicious dog is actually a good thing."
"No, killing a man is wrong — it's bad."

"Why is it wrong?" pressed Prince Andrew. "It's not given to us to know what is right and what is wrong. People always have erred and always will — and in nothing more than in what they consider right and wrong."

"What harms another person is wrong," said Pierre, pleased that for the first time since his arrival Prince Andrew was engaged, had started talking, and wanted to express what had brought him to his present state.
"And who told you what is harmful to another person?" Andrew asked.
"Bad! Bad!" exclaimed Pierre. "We all know what is bad for ourselves."

"Yes, we know that — but the harm I'm aware of in myself is something I can't inflict on others," said Prince Andrew, becoming more and more animated, clearly wanting to express his new outlook to Pierre. He switched to French. "I know only two very real evils in life: remorse and illness. The only good is the absence of those evils. To live for myself, avoiding those two evils — that's my whole philosophy now."

"And love of one's neighbor? And self-sacrifice?" Pierre began. "No, I can't agree with you! To live only so as not to do evil and not to feel regret — that's not enough. I lived like that once, I lived for myself and ruined my life. Only now, when I'm living — or at least trying" — Pierre's modesty made him correct himself — "to live for others, only now have I understood true happiness. No, I can't agree, and you don't really believe what you're saying." Prince Andrew looked at Pierre silently with an ironic smile.

"When you meet my sister — Princess Mary — you'll get along with her," he said. "Perhaps you're right, for yourself," he added after a short pause, "but everyone lives in his own way. You lived for yourself and say you nearly ruined your life and only found happiness when you started living for others. I had just the opposite experience. I lived for glory — and after all, what is glory? The same love of others, a desire to do something for them, a desire for their approval. So I lived for others, and not almost but completely ruined my life. And I've only found some peace since I began living for myself alone."
"But what do you mean by living for yourself alone?" asked Pierre, growing excited. "What about your son, your sister, your father?"

"But that's just the same as myself — they're not others," Prince Andrew explained. "Other people, one's neighbors — le prochain, as you and Princess Mary call it — are the main source of all error and evil. Le prochain — your Kiev peasants you want to do good for."
And he looked at Pierre with a mocking, challenging expression, clearly wanting to draw him out.

"You're joking," replied Pierre, growing more excited. "What error or evil can there be in my wishing to do good — and even doing a little, though I did it badly? What harm is there if unfortunate people — our serfs, people like us — were growing up and dying with no idea of God or truth beyond ceremonies and meaningless prayers, and are now learning a comforting faith in a future life, in retribution, reward, and consolation? What evil is there in providing a doctor, a hospital, and an asylum for the elderly to people who were dying of disease without any help, when such assistance is so easy to give? Isn't it an obvious, undeniable good to give rest and relief to a peasant or a mother with a baby who has no peace day or night?" said Pierre, speaking quickly, with a lisp. "And I've done that — though badly and in small measure — but I have done something, and you can't persuade me it wasn't a good thing. More than that, you can't make me believe you don't think so yourself. And the main thing," he went on, "is that I know — I know for certain — that the joy of doing good is the only sure happiness in life."

"Yes, if you put it that way, it's a different matter entirely," said Prince Andrew. "I build a house and plant a garden, and you build hospitals. Either one can serve as a pastime. But what's truly right and good can only be judged by someone who knows everything — not by us. Well, you want an argument," he added. "Come on, then."
They rose from the table and sat down in the entrance porch, which served as a veranda.

"Let's argue, then," said Prince Andrew. "You talk about schools," he went on, bending a finger, "education and the like — that is, you want to raise him" — he pointed to a peasant passing by who doffed his cap — "out of his animal condition and awaken spiritual needs in him. But it seems to me that animal happiness is the only happiness possible — and that's exactly what you want to take from him. I envy him, but you want to make him into what I am without giving him my resources. Then you say 'lighten his toil.' But as I see it, physical labor is as essential to him, as much a condition of his existence, as mental activity is to you or me. You can't help thinking. I go to bed after two in the morning, thoughts come, and I can't sleep — I toss until dawn because I think and can't stop, just as he can't stop plowing and mowing. If he didn't, he'd go to the tavern or fall sick. Just as I couldn't stand his terrible physical labor and would die within a week, he couldn't stand my idleness — he'd grow fat and die. And the third thing — what else did you mention?" He bent a third finger. "Ah, yes — hospitals, medicine. He has a seizure, he's dying, and you come along and bleed him and patch him up. He'll drag on as a cripple, a burden to everyone, for another ten years. It would be far easier and simpler for him to die. Others are being born — there are plenty as it is. It would be different if you were reluctant to lose a laborer — that's how I see him — but you want to cure him out of love. And he doesn't want that. Besides, what an idea — that medicine ever cured anyone! Killed them, yes!" he said, frowning angrily and turning away from Pierre.

Prince Andrew expressed his views so clearly and precisely that it was obvious he had thought about this at length. He spoke readily and rapidly, like a man who has not talked in a long time. His eyes grew more animated as his conclusions grew more bleak.

"Oh, that's terrible, terrible!" said Pierre. "I can't understand how one can live with such ideas. I had moments like that myself not long ago — in Moscow and while traveling — but at those times I collapsed so completely that I couldn't function, everything seemed hateful to me, myself most of all. Then I couldn't eat, couldn't wash... How is it with you?"

"Why not wash? That's unhygienic," said Prince Andrew. "On the contrary, one should try to make one's life as pleasant as possible. I'm alive — that's not my fault — so I must live out my life as best I can without hurting others."
"But with such views, what motive is there to go on living? One would just sit without moving, doing nothing..."

"Life itself doesn't leave you in peace. I'd be grateful to do nothing, but here on one hand the local nobility have done me the honor of electing me their marshal — I could barely get out of it. They couldn't understand that I lack the necessary qualities — the good-natured, fussy shallowness the job requires. Then there's this house, which has to be built to have a corner of my own for some peace. And now there's the recruiting."
"Why aren't you serving in the army?"

"After Austerlitz!" said Prince Andrew darkly. "No, thank you. I've promised myself never to serve in the active Russian army again. Not even if Bonaparte were here at Smolensk, threatening Bald Hills. Well, as I was saying," he continued, regaining his composure, "now there's the recruiting. My father is chief of the Third District, and my only way of avoiding active service is to serve under him."
"So you are serving?"
"I am."
He was quiet for a moment.
"And why do you serve?"

"For this reason: my father is one of the most remarkable men of his time. But he's growing old, and though not exactly cruel, he has too forceful a temperament. He's so accustomed to unlimited power that he's terrifying, and now he has this authority as a commander in chief of recruitment, granted by the Emperor. If I had been two hours late a couple of weeks ago, he would have had a paymaster's clerk at Yukhnovo hanged," said Prince Andrew with a smile. "So I serve because I'm the only one who has any influence over my father, and now and then I can save him from actions that would torment him afterward."
"Well, there you see!"

"Yes, but it's not the way you think," Prince Andrew continued. "I didn't and don't in the least care about that scoundrel of a clerk who stole boots from the recruits — I would actually have been glad to see him hanged. But I was sorry for my father — and that again is for my own sake."
Prince Andrew grew more and more animated. His eyes glittered feverishly as he tried to prove to Pierre that his actions contained no desire to do good for his neighbor.

"So — you want to liberate your serfs," he continued. "That's a very fine thing, but not for you — I don't suppose you've ever had anyone flogged or sent to Siberia — and still less for your serfs. If they're beaten, flogged, or sent to Siberia, I doubt they're any the worse for it. In Siberia they lead the same animal life, and the welts on their bodies heal, and they're as contented as before. But it's a good thing for the proprietors — who are destroyed morally, who bring remorse upon themselves, stifle that remorse, and grow callous as a result of having the power to punish justly and unjustly. It's those people I pity, and for their sake I would like to liberate the serfs. You may not have seen it, but I have — how good men raised in those traditions of unlimited power, as they grow more irritable with age, become cruel and harsh, know it, but can't control themselves, and grow more and more wretched."
Prince Andrew spoke so passionately that Pierre couldn't help thinking these ideas had been suggested by Prince Andrew's own father's case.
He said nothing in reply.
"So that's what I'm sorry for — human dignity, peace of mind, purity — and not the serfs' backs and foreheads, which, beat and shave them as you might, always remain the same backs and foreheads."
"No, no! A thousand times no! I will never agree with you," said Pierre.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: In the evening, Andrew and Pierre got into the open carriage and drove to Bald Hills. Prince Andrew, glancing at Pierre, broke the silence now and then with remarks that showed he was in a good mood.
Pointing to the fields, he spoke of the improvements he was making to his farming.
Pierre remained gloomily silent, answering in monosyllables, apparently absorbed in his own thoughts.

He was thinking that Prince Andrew was unhappy, that he had lost his way, that he didn't see the true light, and that he, Pierre, ought to help, enlighten, and uplift him. But the moment he considered what he should say, he felt that Prince Andrew would demolish his entire philosophy with a single word, a single argument — and so he shrank from beginning, afraid of exposing what he held sacred to possible ridicule.
"No — but why do you think that?" Pierre suddenly began, lowering his head and looking like a bull about to charge. "Why do you think that? You shouldn't think that way."
"Think? About what?" asked Prince Andrew in surprise.

"About life. About man's destiny. It can't be the way you see it. I used to think the same way, and do you know what saved me? Freemasonry! No, don't smile. Freemasonry is not a religious ceremony or a sect, as I once thought. Freemasonry is the best expression of the best and most eternal aspects of humanity."

And he began to explain Freemasonry as he understood it to Prince Andrew. He said that Freemasonry is the teaching of Christianity freed from the chains of Church and State — a teaching of equality, brotherhood, and love.

"Only our holy brotherhood possesses the real meaning of life; all the rest is a dream," said Pierre. "Understand, my dear fellow, that outside this union everything is filled with deceit and falsehood, and I agree with you that an intelligent, good man has nothing left but to live out his life trying not to hurt others. But make our fundamental convictions your own — join our brotherhood, surrender yourself to us, let yourself be guided, and you will immediately feel, as I have felt, that you are part of a vast, invisible chain whose beginning is hidden in heaven," said Pierre.

Prince Andrew, looking straight ahead, listened in silence. More than once, when the noise of the wheels kept him from catching Pierre's words, he asked him to repeat — and from the particular glow that came into his eyes and his silence, Pierre could tell his words were not in vain, and that Prince Andrew would neither interrupt nor laugh at him.
They reached a river that had overflowed its banks and had to be crossed by ferry. While the carriage and horses were being loaded onto the raft, they stepped on as well.
Prince Andrew leaned on the railing and gazed silently at the floodwaters shimmering in the setting sun.
"Well, what do you think about it?" asked Pierre. "Why are you quiet?"

"What do I think? I'm listening. It's all very well. You say: join our brotherhood and we'll show you the meaning of life, the destiny of man, and the laws that govern the world. But who are we? Human beings. How is it that you know everything? Why am I the only one who can't see what you see? You see a reign of goodness and truth on earth — but I don't."
Pierre interrupted him.
"Do you believe in a future life?" he asked.
"A future life?" Prince Andrew repeated — but Pierre, giving him no time to answer, took the repetition as a denial, all the more readily since he knew of Prince Andrew's former atheism.

"You say you can't see a kingdom of goodness and truth on earth. Neither could I — and it can't be seen if you regard this life as the end of everything. On earth — here on this earth" — Pierre pointed to the fields — "there is no truth; all is false and evil. But in the universe, in the whole universe, there is a kingdom of truth, and we who are now children of the earth are — for all eternity — children of the whole universe. Don't I feel in my soul that I am part of this vast, harmonious whole? Don't I feel that in this immense multitude of beings, in which the Divine — the Supreme Power, if you prefer — is manifest, I form one link, one step, between the lower and the higher? If I see — clearly see — a ladder leading from plant to man, why should I suppose it breaks off at me and doesn't go further and further? I feel that I cannot simply vanish, since nothing in this world vanishes, but that I shall always exist and always have existed. I feel that beyond me and above me there are spirits, and that in this world there is truth."

"Yes, that's Herder's theory," said Prince Andrew, "but it's not arguments that can convince me, dear friend — it's life and death that convince. What convinces is when you see a being dear to you, bound up with your own life, someone before whom you feel guilty and hoped to make amends" — Prince Andrew's voice trembled and he turned away — "and suddenly that being is seized with pain, suffers, and ceases to exist. Why? It cannot be that there is no answer. And I believe there is. That's what convinces — that is what has convinced me," said Prince Andrew.
"Yes, yes, of course," said Pierre. "Isn't that what I'm saying?"

"No. All I say is that it's not arguments that convince me of the necessity of a future life, but this: when you walk hand in hand with someone, and suddenly that person vanishes — into nowhere — and you're left standing before that abyss, staring into it. And I have stared into it."
"Well, that's exactly it! You know that there is a there, and there is a Someone. There is the future life. The Someone is God."

Prince Andrew did not reply. The carriage and horses had long since been taken off the raft and reharnessed on the far bank. The sun had sunk halfway below the horizon and an evening frost was glazing the puddles near the ferry, but Pierre and Andrew — to the astonishment of the footmen, coachmen, and ferrymen — still stood on the raft, talking.

"If there is a God and a future life, there is truth and goodness, and man's highest happiness lies in striving to attain them. We must live, we must love, and we must believe that we live not only today on this scrap of earth, but have lived and shall live forever — there, in the Whole," said Pierre, pointing to the sky.

Prince Andrew stood leaning on the railing, gazing at the red reflection of the sun on the blue water. There was perfect stillness. Pierre fell silent. The raft had long since stopped, and only the gentle waves of the current lapped softly against it. Prince Andrew felt as if the sound of the water was a kind of refrain to Pierre's words, whispering:
"It is true, believe it."
He sighed and looked at Pierre's flushed, enraptured face with a radiant, childlike, tender gaze — one that was also a bit shy before his more assured friend.

"Yes, if only it were so!" said Prince Andrew. "But it's time to go." And stepping off the raft, he looked up at the sky to which Pierre had pointed, and for the first time since Austerlitz he saw that high, everlasting sky he had gazed at on the battlefield; and something that had long been dormant, something that was the best in him, suddenly stirred — joyful and youthful — in his soul. It vanished as soon as he returned to the normal conditions of his life, but he knew that this feeling — which he had no idea how to nurture — existed within him. His meeting with Pierre marked a turning point in Prince Andrew's life. Though outwardly he continued to live as before, inwardly he began a new life.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: It was getting dark when Prince Andrew and Pierre drove up to the front entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrew pointed out with a smile a commotion at the back porch. A woman bent with age, a wallet on her back, and a short, long-haired young man in a black robe had dashed back to the gate on seeing the carriage. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing fearfully at the carriage, hurried up the steps of the back porch.

"Those are Mary's 'God's folk,'" said Prince Andrew. "They've mistaken us for my father. This is the one matter in which she disobeys him. He orders these pilgrims driven away, but she takes them in."
"But what are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
Prince Andrew had no time to answer. The servants came out to greet them, and he asked where the old prince was and whether he was expected back soon.
The old prince had gone to town and was expected any minute.
Prince Andrew led Pierre to his own rooms — which were always kept in perfect order at his father's house — and went to the nursery.

"Let's go see my sister," he said to Pierre when he returned. "I haven't found her yet — she's hiding now, sitting with her 'God's folk.' It'll serve her right; she'll be embarrassed. But you'll see her 'God's folk.' It's really quite something."
"What are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
"Come, and you'll see for yourself."

Princess Mary was indeed flustered, red patches appearing on her face, when they entered. In her cozy room, with lamps burning before the icon stand, a young man with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk's cassock, sat on the sofa beside her, behind a samovar. Nearby in an armchair sat a thin, shriveled old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.
"Andrew, why didn't you warn me?" said the princess, with mild reproach, as she stood before her pilgrims like a hen protecting her chicks.

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
"Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you."
"Ah, and Ivanushka is here too!" said Prince Andrew, glancing with a smile at the young pilgrim.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," Prince Andrew said to Pierre.
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated.
"You must know that this is a woman."
"For heaven's sake."
It was clear that Prince Andrew's ironic attitude toward the pilgrims and Princess Mary's helpless attempts to shield them were their usual, long-established dynamic on this subject.
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew, "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."
"But, my dear, you ought on the contrary to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."

"Really?" said Pierre, peering over his spectacles with curiosity and seriousness — for which Princess Mary was especially grateful — at Ivanushka's face. Ivanushka, sensing she was being discussed, looked around at them all with sly eyes.

Princess Mary's embarrassment on behalf of her guests was quite unnecessary. They were not the least bit flustered. The old woman, eyes lowered but casting sideways glances at the newcomers, had turned her cup upside down and placed a nibbled piece of sugar beside it, sitting quietly in her armchair, clearly hoping for another cup of tea. Ivanushka, sipping from her saucer, watched the young men from under her brows with sly, feminine eyes.
"Where have you been? To Kiev?" Prince Andrew asked the old woman.

"I have, dear sir," she answered readily. "At Christmastime I was found worthy to receive the holy sacrament at the shrine of the saint. And now I've come from Kolyazin, sir, where a great and wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"And was Ivanushka with you?"
"I travel alone, kind sir," said Ivanushka, trying to speak in a bass voice. "I only ran into Pelageya at Yukhnovo."
Pelageya interrupted her companion — she obviously wanted to tell what she had seen.
"In Kolyazin, sir, a wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"What is it? Some new relics?" asked Prince Andrew.
"Andrew, please stop," said Princess Mary. "Don't tell him, Pelageya."

"No, why not, my dear? Why shouldn't I? I like him. He's kind, he's one of God's chosen, a benefactor — he once gave me ten rubles, I remember. When I was in Kiev, Holy Fool Cyril says to me — he's one of God's own, walks barefoot summer and winter — he says, 'Why aren't you going to the right place? Go to Kolyazin, where a miracle-working icon of the Holy Mother of God has been revealed.' Hearing those words, I said goodbye to the holy folk and went."
Everyone was silent; only the pilgrim woman went on in measured tones, drawing in her breath.
"So I come, sir, and the people say to me: 'A great blessing has been revealed — holy oil drips from the cheeks of our Blessed Mother, the Holy Virgin...'"
"All right, all right, you can tell us later," said Princess Mary, blushing.
"Let me ask her," said Pierre. "Did you see it yourself?"
"Oh yes, sir, I was found worthy. Such a brightness on the face, like the light of heaven, and from the Blessed Mother's cheek it drops and drops..."
"But my dear woman, that must be a fraud!" said Pierre naively, having listened attentively to the pilgrim.
"Oh sir! What are you saying?" exclaimed the horrified Pelageya, turning to Princess Mary for support.
"They're imposing on the people," Pierre repeated.

"Lord Jesus Christ!" cried the pilgrim, crossing herself. "Oh, don't say that, sir! There was a general who didn't believe — he said, 'The monks are cheating' — and the moment he said it, he went blind. And he dreamed that the Holy Virgin of the Kiev catacombs came to him and said, 'Believe in me and I will make you whole.' So he begged: 'Take me to her, take me to her.' It's the honest truth — I saw it with my own eyes. They brought him, quite blind, straight to her, and he falls down and says, 'Make me whole, and I'll give you what the Tsar gave me.' I saw it myself, sir — the star is set right into the icon. Well, and then what? He got his sight back! It's a sin to talk like that. God will punish you," she said admonishingly, turning to Pierre.
"How did the star get into the icon?" Pierre asked.
"And was the Holy Mother promoted to the rank of general?" said Prince Andrew with a smile.
Pelageya suddenly went very pale and clasped her hands.

"Oh sir, sir, what a sin! And you who have a son!" she began, her pallor flushing to vivid red. "Sir, what have you said? God forgive you! My dear, what does it mean?" she asked, turning to Princess Mary. She stood up and, nearly in tears, began gathering her things into her wallet. She was clearly frightened and ashamed to have accepted hospitality in a house where such things could be said, and at the same time sorry to lose the charity this house provided.
"Now, why did you have to do that?" said Princess Mary. "Why did you come to me?"

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her. I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
"Princess, on my word, I did not wish to offend her."
Pelageya hesitated, but Pierre's face showed such sincere penitence, and Prince Andrew looked so gently now at her and now at Pierre, that she was gradually reassured.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: The pilgrim woman, once mollified, needed little encouragement to talk at length. She told them about Father Amphilochus, who led so holy a life that his hands smelled of incense, and how on her last visit to Kiev some monks she knew had given her the keys to the catacombs, and how she had taken some dried bread and spent two days among the saints. "I'd pray awhile to one, sit and think awhile, then move on to another. I'd sleep a bit and then go kiss the relics again, and there was such peace all around, such blessedness, that you don't want to come back out — not even into the light of heaven."
Pierre listened attentively and seriously. Prince Andrew left the room, and then — leaving "God's folk" to finish their tea — Princess Mary took Pierre into the drawing room.
"You are very kind," she said to him.
"Oh, I really didn't mean to hurt her feelings. I understand them so well and have the greatest respect for them."
Princess Mary looked at him in silence and smiled affectionately.

"I've known you a long time, you see, and love you like a brother," she said. "How do you find Andrew?" she added quickly, not giving him time to respond to her warm words. "I'm very worried about him. His health was better in winter, but last spring his wound reopened and the doctor said he should go away for treatment. And I'm also very much afraid for him spiritually. He doesn't have a temperament like us women, who can cry away our sorrows. He keeps everything locked inside. Today he's cheerful and in good spirits — but that's the effect of your visit; he's not often like this. If you could persuade him to go abroad... He needs activity, and this quiet, routine life is very bad for him. Others don't notice it, but I see it."
Around ten o'clock the servants rushed to the front door, hearing the bells of the old prince's carriage approaching. Prince Andrew and Pierre also went out to the porch.
"Who's that?" asked the old prince, noticing Pierre as he climbed out of the carriage.
"Ah! Very glad! Give me a kiss," he said, having learned who the young stranger was.
The old prince was in a good mood and very gracious to Pierre.

Before supper, Prince Andrew returned to his father's study and found him hotly debating with their guest. Pierre was arguing that a time would come when there would be no more wars. The old prince challenged him playfully but without getting angry.

"Drain the blood from men's veins and fill them with water, and then there'll be no more war! Old women's nonsense — old women's nonsense!" he repeated, but still patted Pierre affectionately on the shoulder. Then he went to the table where Prince Andrew — obviously not wanting to join the conversation — was looking through the papers his father had brought from town. The old prince came up to him and began talking business.

"The marshal — a Count Rostov — hasn't sent half his quota. He came to town and wanted to invite me to dinner — I gave him a fine dinner! And then, look at this... Well, my boy," the old prince went on, turning to his son and patting Pierre on the shoulder, "a fine fellow, your friend — I like him! He gets me going. Another man says clever things and you don't care to listen, but this one talks nonsense and stirs an old man up. Well, go on! Get along! Maybe I'll come sit with you at supper. We'll have another argument. Make friends with my little fool, Princess Mary," he shouted after Pierre through the door.

Only now, on this visit to Bald Hills, did Pierre fully appreciate the strength and charm of his friendship with Prince Andrew. That charm showed itself not so much in his relationship with Andrew as in his interactions with the whole family and household. With the stern old prince and the gentle, timid Princess Mary — though he barely knew them — Pierre immediately felt like an old friend. They were all fond of him already. Not only Princess Mary, who had been won over by his kindness to the pilgrims and now gave him her most radiant looks, but even the one-year-old "Prince Nicholas" (as his grandfather called him) smiled at Pierre and let himself be held; and Michael Ivanovich and Mademoiselle Bourienne beamed with pleasant smiles when he talked to the old prince.
The old prince came to supper — clearly on Pierre's account. And during the two days of the young man's visit, he was extremely warm and told him to come again.

When Pierre had gone and the household gathered together, they began sharing their impressions of him, as people always do after a new acquaintance has left — but as rarely happens, no one said anything but good of him.
